chapters.title: Chapter 2: Reading Where India Is in the Cycle

lessons.title: Building a Simple Business Cycle Scorecard

body.text: A scorecard will not tell you the future. What it does is force you to look at the same evidence, the same way, every month, so your view of the cycle changes when the data changes, not when the headlines do.

children.text: Lessons 2.1 to 2.3 gave you the parts: leading and coincident indicators, credit, capacity, the yield curve, and the RBI clock. This lesson assembles them into a one-page scorecard you can update in about twenty minutes a month. By the end, you will score India's actual position as of September 2026, and you will know exactly which readings would change that call.
Why Bother With a Scorecard?
Because your brain is a poor cycle detector. Left to judgement alone, most investors fall into the same traps.
Recency bias: the last month's data, or the last week's market move, dominates the view.
Headline bias: one dramatic number, like a record GDP print, overwhelms five quieter signals pointing the other way.
Confirmation bias: you notice the indicators that support the sector tilt you already own.
Single-indicator faith: "the yield curve says recession" or "credit growth is strong, all is well", ignoring that every signal gives false alarms.
A fixed set of indicators, scored with fixed rules, protects you from all four. It will sometimes be wrong. But it will be wrong consistently and transparently, which means you can learn from it.
Step 1: Choose a Small Set of Indicators
More indicators do not mean more accuracy; they mean more noise and more room to cherry pick. This scorecard uses five growth indicators to place the cycle, plus a separate three-part policy dial.

cells: Breadth and direction of factory activity; leading
HSBC / S&P Global, first working day of the month
Breadth and direction of services activity, the bigger part of GDP
HSBC / S&P Global, third working day
The broadest measure of activity; coincident, released late
MoSPI, about two months after the quarter
Whether a capex cycle is being triggered
RBI OBICUS, quarterly with a long lag
Policy dial: RBI stance, yield curve, CPI inflation
Whether policy is a tailwind or a headwind

children.text: Step 2: Score Each Indicator on Level and Direction

Every indicator gets two scores. The level score asks whether the reading is strong, normal, or weak. The direction score asks whether it is improving or deteriorating compared with an earlier reading. Keeping them separate is the whole trick, because the four phases of the cycle are defined by exactly those two questions.

body.caption: Scoring rules (rules of thumb, adjust as data series change)

cells: +1 if higher than the previous reading, -1 if lower, 0 if unchanged
Compare with the same quarter a year earlier

body.text: These thresholds are simple teaching benchmarks, not official definitions. The PMI threshold of 54 sits close to the manufacturing PMI's long-run average of about 54.2. The GDP band assumes India's trend growth is roughly 6% to 7%, which is an estimate, and India's new GDP series with base year 2022-23 may shift what "normal" growth looks like. Revisit your thresholds once a year, and never change them mid-month to fit a view you already hold.

children.text: Step 3: Map the Scores to a Phase
Now place the two totals on a simple grid. It is the same four-phase cycle from Lesson 1.1, defined by where activity is and where it is heading.

cells: Level 0 or above (at or above trend)

children.text: Treat scores close to the boundaries with humility. A level of 0 with momentum of +1 is a borderline call that could flip next month. A level of +4 with momentum of +4 is a strong one. The size of the scores matters as much as the quadrant.
Step 4: Add the Policy Dial
The phase tells you where the economy is. The policy dial tells you whether the RBI and the bond market are pushing with the cycle or against it, which matters enormously for rate sensitive sectors.

Add the three components. A total of +2 or +3 is a policy tailwind, -2 or -3 is a headwind, and anything in between is neutral. Always read the dial with its story, not just its score. A steep curve because the RBI has cut is a tailwind; a steep curve because long yields are rising on inflation fears is much less friendly.
Worked Example: India in September 2026
Here is the scorecard filled in with the latest data available in mid September 2026.

body.title: September 2026 scorecard: level and direction by indicator

stats.label: Phase
stats.context: Level at or above 0, momentum above 0

stats.label: Policy dial
stats.context: Stance neutral (0), curve about 175 bps (+1), CPI 4.82% (0)

children.text: The scorecard places India firmly in expansion: a level score of +4 and momentum of +3. Growth of 7.8% in April to June 2026, fixed investment up 11.9% in that quarter, credit growth nearly double its level of a year earlier, and utilisation in the capex trigger zone all describe a broad, investment-led upswing.

But read the details, not just the total. Three signals are the kind that tend to appear as an expansion matures. Manufacturing PMI is the one growth indicator deteriorating, with new orders and output growing at their weakest pace in five years. CPI inflation rose to 4.82% in August, a seven-month high and above the 4% target. And the steep yield curve is not the friendly kind: the 10-year yield has risen about half a percentage point over the year amid higher crude oil prices, while the RBI sits on hold. The policy dial scores neutral today, but the direction of its components points towards a future headwind rather than a tailwind.

body.text: This worked example is a teaching snapshot, not a forecast or a recommendation. The capacity utilisation reading is already nine months old, GDP and credit figures will be revised, and every reading here will be out of date within weeks. The point is the method: rerun the scorecard each month with fresh data, and pay most attention to which scores change.

body.title: Go deeper: making the scorecard sturdier without overfitting

children.text: Use three-month averages for noisy monthly data such as PMI and auto sales, so one odd month does not flip a direction score.
Compare direction over a consistent window. Mixing month-on-month for one indicator and year-on-year for another is acceptable only if you apply the same rule every month.
Weight carefully, or not at all. It is tempting to give extra weight to whichever indicator worked best last cycle. That is how scorecards get overfitted to the past and fail in the next cycle.

Log the score every month. A simple spreadsheet with dates, readings, scores, and your one-line interpretation is the most valuable part of the exercise, because it shows how the phase evolved and how early or late your calls were.

Keep a separate "watch list" of warning signs outside the score, such as credit spreads widening, an RBI stance change, or a jump in crude oil prices, so they inform your judgement without muddying the core scores.
Practice

body.title: Score the Momentum
body.prompt: A hypothetical dashboard shows: manufacturing PMI 49.2 (previous reading 51.5), services PMI 51.0 (previously 53.0), real GDP growth 6.1% (7.2% a year earlier), non-food credit growth 11% (15% a year earlier), and capacity utilisation 76% (77.5% the previous quarter). Using the scoring rules in this lesson, what is the momentum score?
body.explanation: Every one of the five indicators is lower than its comparison reading, so each scores -1 for direction, giving a momentum score of -5. Momentum that is uniformly negative is a strong signal, even before you look at the levels.

body.title: Place the Phase
body.question: For the same hypothetical dashboard, the level scores are: manufacturing PMI -1 (below 50), services PMI 0, GDP 0, credit 0, and capacity utilisation +1. That gives a level score of 0 and a momentum score of -5. Which phase does the scorecard indicate?
body.explanation: A level score of 0 is at the trend boundary, so the economy is not yet below trend, while momentum of -5 shows every indicator deteriorating. Level at or above 0 with momentum at or below 0 maps to slowdown. If the next few readings push levels below 0 while momentum stays negative, the scorecard would move to contraction.

body.title: Complete the Grid
body.textWithBlank: On the scorecard grid, a level score below 0 combined with a momentum score above 0 indicates the ___ phase.
body.explanation: Below trend but improving is recovery: activity is still weak in level terms, but more indicators are getting better than worse. This is typically when markets have already started to turn, as Lesson 1.3 showed.

body.title: Complete the Scorecard
body.scenario: Continue with the hypothetical dashboard above. In addition, the RBI has kept the repo rate unchanged for three meetings after a hiking cycle and holds a neutral stance. The 10-year G-sec yields 7.1% and the 91-day T-bill yields 6.7%. CPI inflation is 5.8%. You own a portfolio tilted towards capital goods and metals, bought during the last expansion.
body.prompt: Score the policy dial, state the overall read, and explain what the scorecard suggests you should review in your portfolio.
body.modelAnswer: Policy dial: stance neutral and on hold scores 0; the term spread is 7.1% minus 6.7%, or 40 bps, which is below 50 bps and scores -1; CPI of 5.8% is between 4% and 6% and scores 0. The dial totals -1, neutral but leaning towards headwind, and a flat curve with inflation near the top of the band limits how quickly the RBI can cut. Overall read: slowdown, with every growth indicator deteriorating, manufacturing PMI already below 50, and capacity utilisation starting to roll over from high levels. That is the classic late-cycle setup for capital goods and metals, where new capacity arrives as demand cools. The scorecard does not say sell. It says review: check whether order books and earnings estimates for your holdings are being cut, whether the position sizes still make sense if the slowdown deepens, and which defensive or rate sensitive sectors might benefit once the RBI eventually turns to cuts. Then rerun the scorecard next month to see whether the slowdown is deepening or stabilising.

body.label: MoSPI: Official Data Releases
body.description: GDP, CPI, and IIP releases and the advance release calendar, to keep your monthly scorecard updated with official data.

body.text: This scorecard is an educational framework, not an investment recommendation or a forecasting model. The thresholds are simplified rules of thumb, the September 2026 example uses data that will be revised and superseded, and no scorecard reliably predicts the cycle or market returns.

points: A scorecard protects you from recency, headline, and confirmation bias by applying the same rules to the same indicators every month
Use a small set of indicators: manufacturing PMI, services PMI, real GDP growth, non-food credit growth, and capacity utilisation
Score each indicator separately on level (strong, normal, weak) and direction (improving or deteriorating)
Level at or above 0 with improving momentum is expansion; with deteriorating momentum it is slowdown; below 0 and improving is recovery; below 0 and deteriorating is contraction
A separate policy dial, combining RBI stance, the yield curve, and CPI inflation, shows whether policy is a tailwind or headwind
As of September 2026, the scorecard reads expansion (level +4, momentum +3) with a neutral policy dial, but cooling manufacturing, rising inflation, and higher bond yields are worth watching
Log your scores monthly and focus on which scores change; the trend in the scorecard matters more than any single month's phase label
